title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to a self-hosted, free alternative. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch from Jira to Plane to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid tool with a per-user monthly fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: With Plane, teams have full control over their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, while Jira is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large, complex projects, while Plane is better suited for smaller teams and projects.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane uses a third-party plugin for Git integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Native integration with Git and other Atlassian tools
* Scalable and suitable for large projects
* Good customer support
* Expensive, especially for large teams
**Plane:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data
* Customizable and flexible
* Suitable for small to medium-sized teams
* Limited scalability and support for large projects
* Requires technical expertise to set up and configure

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams or projects that require a high level of scalability and support. It is also a good option for teams that are already invested in the Atlassian ecosystem and want to take advantage of native integrations with other tools. On the other hand, Plane is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that want a free, self-hosted solution and are willing to invest time and technical expertise in setting it up and configuring it.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane instance on your own server.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your Jira data.
4. Configure Plane to match your team's workflow and needs.
5. Test and refine your Plane setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's Git integration is not as seamless as Jira's. However, for small to medium-sized teams that want a free, self-hosted solution, Plane is a good option. We recommend switching to Plane if you are a small team with simple project management needs and are willing to invest time in setting it up and configuring it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) with simple project management needs
* Teams that do not need native Git integration
* Teams that want full control over their data and are willing to invest time in setting up and configuring Plane
* Teams that are currently using Jira and are looking to reduce costs
* Teams that are comfortable with self-hosting and technical configuration

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted. You will need to pay for server costs, but there are no per-user fees.
### Can I use Plane for large projects?
No, Plane is not suitable for large, complex projects. It is better suited for small to medium-sized teams and projects.
### Does Plane have native Git integration?
No, Plane uses a third-party plugin for Git integration. This means that the integration is not as seamless as Jira's native Git integration.
### Can I export my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Is Plane production-ready?
Not yet. While Plane is a promising tool, it still lacks some of the features and polish of Jira.
meta_description: Plane, a free self-hosted project management tool, offers an alternative to Jira. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

# Trello vs WeKan (2026)

## Overview
Trello and WeKan are both project management tools that help teams organize and manage their tasks and workflows. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Trello to WeKan, particularly those who value data ownership and self-hosting capabilities. * Cost: Trello offers a free plan with limited features, while WeKan is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: WeKan allows users to host their data on their own servers, giving them full control and ownership.
* Setup complexity: Trello is generally easier to set up and use, while WeKan requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Trello is designed to scale with large teams, while WeKan's scalability depends on the user's server capabilities.
* Integration: Trello has a wider range of integrations with third-party tools, while WeKan has limited integrations but is highly customizable.

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |

### Trello
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Scalable and reliable
* Mobile apps available

### WeKan

WeKan, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own server. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams who require a high degree of customization and control over their workflow.

However, for teams who value data ownership and control, WeKan is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Trello to WeKan if you have a small to medium-sized team and don't require a wide range of integrations with third-party tools.

* Small teams (less than 10 users) who value data ownership and control

### Is WeKan scalable?

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Dropbox is one of the original cloud storage services offering simple file sync. Nextcloud is the most popular self-hosted cloud platform combining file storage, calendar, contacts, video calls, and 400+ apps.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Dropbox charges $9.99-$16.58/user/month; Nextcloud is free to self-host
- **Storage**: Nextcloud storage is limited only by your server disk space
- **Feature breadth**: Nextcloud is far more than storage; it is a full Google Workspace alternative
- **Privacy**: Nextcloud on your own server means only you can access your data
- **Setup**: Dropbox is instant; Nextcloud requires Docker setup

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$500/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,998/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Dropbox

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Dropbox if:** Dropbox suits individuals or small teams wanting simple reliable file sync with no infrastructure to manage.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud suits privacy-focused organizations wanting to eliminate cloud subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Download all Dropbox files locally, then upload to Nextcloud via the web interface or desktop sync client.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Dropbox tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Dropbox, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Dropbox until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Dropbox paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Dropbox to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Dropbox data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Dropbox](https://dropbox.com) and [Nextcloud](https://nextcloud.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Nextcloud is a free, self-hosted alternative to Dropbox. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.
